Call chambers at 806-468-3832 to flag it, and be ready to have a judge’s copy promptly delivered to the Clerk’s office if chambers asks.

docs.t: Judge Lee Ann Reno (N.D. Tex.) — Paper copies
docs.x: Judge Lee Ann Reno, N.D. Tex.. Paper copies: Paper copies of e-filed documents are generally not required; Judge Reno’s scheduling orders set the paper-copy requirements, and chambers may request copies of a specific motion, brief, or appendix and will coordinate timing with counsel.

docs.t: Judge Lee Ann Reno (N.D. Tex.) — Attorney and litigant conduct
docs.x: Judge Lee Ann Reno, N.D. Tex.. Attorney and litigant conduct: By litigating before Judge Reno, counsel and pro se parties represent that they have read and will follow Dondi Properties Corp. v. Commerce Savings & Loan Ass’n, 121 F.R.D. 284 (N.D. Tex. 1988), the Local Civil or Criminal Rules, the Texas Lawyer’s Creed, and the Texas Rules of Professional Conduct.

docs.t: Judge Lee Ann Reno (N.D. Tex.) — Courtroom dress
docs.x: Judge Lee Ann Reno, N.D. Tex.. Courtroom dress: Under LR 83.16 and LCrR 53.2, no shorts, flip flops, tank tops, halter tops, T-shirts with graphic writing, hats, sunglasses, or tights/athletic wear in the courtroom.

docs.t: Judge Lee Ann Reno (N.D. Tex.) — Contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Lee Ann Reno, N.D. Tex.. Contacting chambers: Civil: non-substantive procedural questions not answered by the Federal Rules, Local Civil Rules, or the court’s orders may go to chambers at 806-468-3832. Criminal: direct all questions to the courtroom deputy, Danny Aguilera, at 806-468-3821 (direct) or 806-468-3800 (main).

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Rule 16 conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Rule 16 conference (trap): The judge routinely holds a preliminary pretrial conference. Lead and/or local counsel and pro se parties should expect to appear in person; leave to appear by phone will not be granted absent extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Oral argument and discovery motions
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Oral argument and discovery motions: Discovery motions are routinely set for hearing on an expedited basis. Argument on other motions is allowed case by case; tell the court if you believe argument would be particularly helpful.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Conference before motions
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Conference before motions: Before any nondispositive motion, confer with every affected party to learn whether it is opposed, and include a L.R. 7.1(b) certificate of conference. Not required for motions to dismiss, for judgment on the pleadings, or for summary judgment, or when a conference is not possible.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Proposed orders and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Proposed orders and courtesy copies: Submit proposed orders through ECF. No paper copies of electronically filed documents are required.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — ECF enrollment required (trap)
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. ECF enrollment required (trap): All counsel and self-represented parties must enroll in the court’s ECF system; email and phone communications are not official filings and are not part of the record.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Local counsel and sealing
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Local counsel and sealing: L.R. 83.10 is strictly enforced: local counsel is required whenever lead counsel neither resides nor keeps a principal office in the district, and proceeding without one requires leave by written motion. Do not unreasonably file under seal: file unsealed as much as you reasonably can consistent with any protective order. Redact Social Security and taxpayer-ID numbers, financial-account numbers, minors’ names, and dates of birth.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Contacting chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Contacting chambers (trap): Except in rare emergencies or as directed, do not email the court or any staff, and do not bring procedural or scheduling questions answered by the rules, the scheduling order, or prior orders. Staff will not discuss substance, motion status, or the court’s preferences, or predict rulings. For extenuating circumstances on a pending motion, e-file a notice or request for relief.

docs.t: Judge Rebecca Rutherford (N.D. Tex.) — Consent to magistrate judge
docs.x: Judge Rebecca Rutherford, N.D. Tex.. Consent to magistrate judge: In a case preliminarily assigned to Judge Rutherford, parties may consent under 28 U.S.C. § 636(c) through the ECF electronic-consent option; consent is voluntary and may be withheld without adverse substantive consequences.

docs.t: Judge Reed O’Connor (N.D. Tex.) — Judge’s copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Reed O’Connor, N.D. Tex.. Judge’s copies (trap): A paper judge’s copy is required for each dispositive motion, response, reply, and appendix that exceeds 75 pages. The copy must be in a three-ring binder, with exhibits or attachments appropriately tabbed.

docs.t: Judge Reed O’Connor (N.D. Tex.) — Proposed orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Reed O’Connor, N.D. Tex.. Proposed orders (trap): All motions require a proposed order, emailed to OConnor_Orders@txnd.uscourts.gov in WordPerfect or Word format (not PDF). The email subject line must include the case number and the document number of the motion.

docs.t: Judge Reed O’Connor (N.D. Tex.) — Criminal guilty pleas
docs.x: Judge Reed O’Connor, N.D. Tex.. Criminal guilty pleas: The U.S. Attorney and any charged defendant must file all paperwork related to a guilty plea on the docket without delay, so the plea can be promptly scheduled and heard.

docs.t: Judge Reed O’Connor (N.D. Tex.) — Courtroom and contact
docs.x: Judge Reed O’Connor, N.D. Tex.. Courtroom and contact: Fort Worth, 501 West 10th Street, 2nd-floor courtroom; case letter designation (O). Courtroom deputy Melissa Hurtado (817-850-6788, Melissa_Hurtado@txnd.uscourts.gov).

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Status report and scheduling (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Status report and scheduling (trap): No Rule 26(f) meeting is required as such, but counsel and unrepresented parties must confer and file one joint status report (no separate filings) within 29 days of the Status Report Order, stating positions on consent to a magistrate judge. The scheduling order follows, unless a Rule 16(a) conference is set.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Typical deadlines
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Typical deadlines: Joinder and amendment motions within 90 days of the scheduling order. Discovery closes 150 days before trial, subject to agreed extensions, but the judge will not hear discovery disputes arising from agreed extensions. Experts: plaintiff designates 90 days and defendant or third parties 60 days before the discovery deadline; rebuttal experts within 30 days of the other side’s disclosure; expert challenges 90 days before trial. Summary judgment and all other dispositive motions within 14 days after the discovery deadline; delay in ruling will not move the trial date.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Settlement (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Settlement (trap): File a joint settlement report within 90 days of the scheduling order describing negotiations and specific efforts (or why none occurred). Parties and lead counsel must meet in person or by phone at least 21 days before trial to discuss settlement, then immediately notify the court in writing of the participants’ names and capacities and the result.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Motions and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Motions and proposed orders: Rulings are usually on the briefs; oral argument may be set on request or sua sponte. Reasonable uncontested motions are usually granted but must include an agreed order or certificate of conference stating the motion is unopposed. Email proposed orders in Word to Lindsay_Orders@txnd.uscourts.gov. Continuances and other motions follow the Local Rules and Federal Rules.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Courtesy copies and deliveries (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Courtesy copies and deliveries (trap): In criminal cases, mail or deliver a timely courtesy copy if a main document has more than three attachments or exhibits, or if the main document or an attachment exceeds 25 pages. Otherwise courtesy copies only as the court’s Standing Order Regarding Electronically Filed Documents requires or chambers requests. No hand deliveries to chambers without permission; deliver to the Clerk’s office and have the item stamped “Received.” No faxes unless chambers directs.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Pretrial filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Pretrial filings (trap): Rule 26(a)(3) materials, witness lists, proposed voir dire, and proposed jury instructions and verdict form are due 21 days before trial. Witness lists must give a brief narrative of each witness’s testimony, say whether the witness was deposed, and label the testimony “probable,” “possible,” “expert,” or “record custodian.” Objections to exhibits and deposition excerpts may be filed 10 days before trial, after the parties confer. The joint pretrial order is due 21 days before trial, prepared by plaintiff’s counsel (defense counsel helps if plaintiff is pro se) and submitted as a proposed order under the CM/ECF procedures; one filed without the judge’s signature will be unfiled. The final pretrial conference is usually 3 to 7 days before trial. Motions in limine are due 21 days before trial, heard at the pretrial conference, and m

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Exhibits
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Exhibits: Exhibits go in labeled three-ring binders (“Plaintiff’s/Defendant’s Exhibit Notebook,” with case style and number), with a title page, an exhibit index, and tabs; standard exhibit labels are fine. Deliver to chambers one set for the judge in a jury trial, or one set for the judge and one for the law clerk in a bench trial.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Trial: The judge generally conducts voir dire, with brief follow-up by the parties on areas not covered; time is set case by case. Opening statements may be limited, generally to 15–30 minutes per side; exhibits may be used in openings only if all parties agree. Evidence presentation usually has no time limit. Electronic presentation is strongly encouraged; set it up before trial, and training is required. The court provides no blackboards, chart stands, overhead projectors, video equipment, or easels. In bench trials, the parties order and split the cost of the transcript, then file proposed findings (each with a record cite) and conclusions (each with authority) within 30 days after the transcript is completed.

docs.t: Judge Sam A. Lindsay (N.D. Tex.) — Decorum and contact
docs.x: Judge Sam A. Lindsay, N.D. Tex.. Decorum and contact: Address the judge as “Your Honor” or “Judge Lindsay” and others by last name; use the podium when addressing a witness. Only water is allowed; no gum or newspapers. Staff may be called about procedural, not substantive, matters (civil: Dedrea Kearney, 214-753-2365; criminal: Tannica Stewart, 214-753-2368). Attorneys may ask to speak with the judge with both sides present.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Motions (trap): No briefing orders are entered. The court entertains only motions and responses, with no replies unless ordered. Motions are decided on the briefs without hearing unless the court orders otherwise. Proposed agreed orders are not considered without an underlying motion; they need not be signed by counsel or parties, as the court relies on the certificate of conference in the unopposed motion. In removed cases, motions filed in state court must be re-urged to be before the court. Motions for continuance are rarely granted.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Case management: No preliminary pretrial conference, no Rule 26(f) conference, no status report, and (unless ordered) no Rule 26(a)(1) initial disclosures. The scheduling order sets deadlines to join parties, amend pleadings, and file summary judgment motions, and sets the trial date. Electronic filing is not mandatory. There is no docket call: counsel must stay in contact with chambers to learn where the case stands on the docket.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Pretrial order (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Pretrial order (trap): Counsel jointly prepare a proposed pretrial order, due at least 21 days before trial, with a summary of claims and defenses, stipulated facts, a trial-length estimate, other helpful matters, each counsel’s signature, and a signature line for the court. Attach a certificate signed by counsel that they conferred, the stipulations are agreed, and the order is submitted for entry. Disagreement is no excuse for not filing; include each side’s version instead. A final pretrial conference is held only at the court’s discretion; if you think one is needed, notify chambers no later than when the proposed pretrial order is filed.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Trial deadlines
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Trial deadlines: At least 21 days before trial: Rule 26(a)(3) disclosures, exchange of exhibits, and filing and service of proposed jury instructions and issues (jury cases) or proposed findings and conclusions (non-jury cases).

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Discovery: Counsel must strictly comply with Dondi Properties Corp. v. Commerce Savings & Loan Ass’n, 121 F.R.D. 284 (N.D. Tex. 1988) (en banc), and cooperate in discovery. Where the case is e-filed, written discovery may be served and answered by email.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Trial procedure (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Trial procedure (trap): Lawyers may not submit proposed voir dire questions; after the judge’s voir dire, each party gets thirty minutes of supplemental questions, with no opening statements at that stage unless the court asks. Jury-trial openings are limited to thirty minutes per party; non-jury trials usually have no openings or closings. Only direct, cross, and limited redirect are allowed. Admitted exhibits stay on the table in front of the bench, with documents kept in a ring binder. During deliberations, all counsel must remain in the courthouse and be readily accessible.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Courtroom decorum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Courtroom decorum (trap): Examine witnesses from the lectern; never move the lectern or its microphone. Ask permission to approach a witness or the easel. No briefcases, boxes, or exhibits on counsel tables, benches, or the chairs behind them; no food, drink (including water), tobacco, or gum; and no two-wheeled carts or dollies in the courtroom.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Attorney fees and criminal pleas
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Attorney fees and criminal pleas: Fee applications must follow Johnson v. Georgia Highway Express, Inc., 488 F.2d 714, 717–19 (5th Cir. 1974), and are submitted by affidavits and controverting affidavits. For re-arraignment and guilty pleas, all documents, including plea agreements and factual resumes, must be reviewed by counsel and signed by all parties at least three (3) days before the re-arraignment.

docs.t: Judge Sam R. Cummings (N.D. Tex.) — Contact, copies, and conflicts
docs.x: Judge Sam R. Cummings, N.D. Tex.. Contact, copies, and conflicts: Courtesy copies only if the court requests them. Faxed filings are not accepted. Pretrial and procedural questions not answered by the rules or orders go to the Judicial Assistant at 806-472-1922; law clerks do not take calls from lawyers or litigants. Vacation letters are not recognized; raise conflicts by a motion for extension or continuance.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Rule 26(f) conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Rule 26(f) conference (trap): Lead counsel (or an attorney designee with authority) must meet in person at a mutually agreeable location, unless a party is pro se. The judge does not follow L.R. 16.1(f): cases with pro se plaintiffs must still comply with Rule 16(b) scheduling and planning.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Scheduling proposal
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Scheduling proposal: After most defendants answer or after removal, a scheduling proposal order issues. The joint proposal must state, under a separate heading, whether all parties consent to a magistrate judge (without identifying who does not), and propose deadlines for joinder, amendment, motions, discovery, and expert designations and disclosures. Disagreements must show each side’s position and why agreement failed. Do not submit it as a proposed order. A prior Rule 26(f) report doesn’t excuse the proposal, though it may be adopted by reference if attached. A separate settlement status heading is required; a rote statement that settlement was discussed is unacceptable, and settlement figures may not be disclosed in nonjury cases.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Motions and hearings: No oral argument on motions unless the judge directs (L.R. 7.1(g)). Motion deadlines come from the scheduling and trial docket setting orders, including for summary judgment. Required proposed orders go in a modifiable format to Fitzwater_Orders@txnd.uscourts.gov. No judge’s copy is required unless requested.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Proposed-orders mailbox (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Proposed-orders mailbox (trap): Use Fitzwater_Orders@txnd.uscourts.gov only for proposed orders or when instructed; anything else sent there is discarded without docketing. If a civil case has settled pending final papers, email a letter to that address; the case will be administratively closed meanwhile.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Motions in limine (trap): Not to be filed as a matter of course. Limit them to matters that cannot be raised by trial objection without prejudice and whose mention cannot be cured by instruction; no “standard” requests or disguised substantive motions. Deadlines are set in each case.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Pretrial order and conference
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Pretrial order and conference: A single joint proposed pretrial order, signed by counsel for each party, is due at least 14 days before trial and is emailed in WordPerfect or Word to Fitzwater_Orders. Objections to an opponent’s portions are noted inside the joint order. The pretrial conference, by phone or in person, is usually no later than the week before trial. All civil cases are tried under time limits, and the court will give notice if they significantly cut the parties’ estimate.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Exhibits, voir dire, and instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Exhibits, voir dire, and instructions (trap): Exchange marked exhibits at least 14 days before the trial setting. Exhibits, including demonstratives, must be listed even if not offered into evidence; the impeachment exception is read narrowly. Don’t deliver exhibits to the court or reporter before trial actually begins unless told otherwise. Proposed voir dire, jury instructions and questions, or proposed findings and conclusions are due 14 days before trial, with Word or WordPerfect versions emailed to Fitzwater_Orders. The judge conducts voir dire, with one attorney per side allowed follow-up, usually 10 minutes; questionnaires are not normally permitted. Examination is limited to direct, cross, one redirect, and one recross without leave, and cross follows Rule 611(b). For equipment, contact court coordinator Pat Esquivel, (214) 753-2336.

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Contacting chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Contacting chambers (trap): Never contact the law clerks; they don’t take calls. Use the Chambers Online Help Desk (copying opposing counsel unless there’s a reason not to) or the court coordinator; check motion status with the ECF Help Desk, (214) 753-2633. The help desk is not for emergency filings. Faxed filings are accepted only in rare emergencies. The page states that electronic filing is permitted rather than required (L.R. 5.1(e), L.Crim.R. 49.2(f)).

docs.t: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater (N.D. Tex.) — Criminal discovery protocol
docs.x: Judge Sidney A. Fitzwater, N.D. Tex.. Criminal discovery protocol: The posted district protocol calls for an early meet-and-confer on discovery volume and format, inspection of productions within 21 days, and a good-faith conference before any discovery motion, which must state the dispute couldn’t be resolved.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Judge’s paper copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Judge’s paper copies (trap): A paper copy of every electronically filed document must reach chambers by mail or personal delivery within three working days of filing, or the filing may be unfiled. Faxed or emailed copies are not accepted. The same applies to the magistrate judge’s copy in referred matters. Staple the notice of electronic filing to the upper left corner. Bind: 50 pages or fewer, staple upper left; more than 50 up to 150, two-hole punch at the top in an Acco-type fastener; more than 150, three-hole punch on the left in a 3-ring binder of no more than about 300 pages, with the notice on top inside the first binder and tabbed dividers between exhibits.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Appendices and citations (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Appendices and citations (trap): Underline (or bracket in the margin, for long passages) the parts of an e-filed appendix you rely on; for a manually filed appendix, highlight, underline, or bracket them. Exhibit tabs go on the right side, not the bottom. Attach copies of any non-published cases cited to the appendix. Westlaw citations are preferred over Lexis.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Motions and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Motions and proposed orders: Hearings are set only when the court finds one necessary, so the motion, response, and reply must contain everything needed for a ruling. All motions require a proposed order, emailed in Word or WordPerfect to Means_orders@txnd.uscourts.gov. In criminal cases, say in the subject line whether a continuance order relates to trial, sentencing, or another hearing, and always include the defendant number (use 1 for single-defendant cases).

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Summary judgment (trap): Treat L.R. 56.3(b) and 56.4(b) as saying “must” instead of “may”: everything required by L.R. 56.3(a) and 56.4(a) must be in the brief. Timing is set by the Initial Scheduling Order. The movant must identify, in a separate section at the start of the brief, each appearing party’s live pleadings by name, filing date, and docket number; the response must say whether it agrees and, if not, why.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Scheduling and case management
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Scheduling and case management: After all or most defendants answer, the court issues an Order to Submit a Joint Status Report; the Initial Scheduling Order follows, usually without a conference unless a party requests one. A prior Rule 26(f) report does not replace the Joint Status Report, but portions can be adopted by attaching a copy. The Joint Status Report must say whether the parties will consent to a magistrate judge, without identifying who will or won’t. Most discovery motions are referred to the magistrate judge. Initial disclosures are required unless the parties stipulate otherwise. Do not file discovery materials unless the judge directs.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Continuances and vacation letters (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Continuances and vacation letters (trap): Absent exceptional circumstances, civil continuances are not granted, because the trial month is agreed at the trial-setting conference (see LR 40.1). Vacation letters are not recognized; counsel must monitor settings and move for an extension or continuance if a conflict arises.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Settlement and pretrial
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Settlement and pretrial: The Initial Scheduling Order requires a face-to-face settlement conference; notify the court immediately of any settlement, and an agreed dismissal deadline will be set. Within 60 days after discovery closes, an order for a trial-setting conference issues; the law clerk conducts it, and the Final Scheduling Order says whether a pretrial order is needed. Motions in limine are due about one month before trial, and exhibits are marked and exchanged about one week before the trial month. The final pretrial conference is usually held the morning trial begins. Any exhibit (other than impeachment) to be offered or used as a demonstrative must be exchanged and listed under LR 26.2; the impeachment exception is construed narrowly.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Trial: The judge conducts voir dire and usually gives each side 10 to 15 minutes. Time limits are imposed on evidence under Misc. Order No. 46, examination is limited to direct, cross, and redirect without leave, and cross is limited to the scope under Rule 611(b).

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Courtroom decorum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Courtroom decorum (trap): Stand when court opens or recesses, when the jury enters or leaves, and when addressing or addressed by the court; examine witnesses and argue from the lectern; ask before approaching the bench. Address remarks to the court and refer to everyone by surname. One attorney per witness; the attorney objecting on direct handles cross. Do not confer with your witness once tendered for cross until redirect. State only legal grounds for objections, don’t repeat witness answers, and make stipulation offers out of the jury’s hearing. In opening and closing, no personal opinions (“I think”) and no reading from transcripts. No gestures or audible reactions at counsel table, no food or drink except bottled water, and no gum.

docs.t: Judge Terry R. Means (N.D. Tex.) — Contact and admissions
docs.x: Judge Terry R. Means, N.D. Tex.. Contact and admissions: Case inquiries go to the judicial assistant/courtroom deputy, Michelle Moon (817-850-6670); ECF questions to the Fort Worth (817-850-6733) or Dallas (214-753-2633) help desk. Do not call the law clerks, and don’t ask staff questions answered by the rules or orders. Bar admission oaths are by appointment only (817-850-6670), generally on 10:00 a.m. criminal docket days; present papers in Room 502 by 9:45 a.m. with a sponsoring member of the bar.

docs.t: Judge David Wayne Dugan (S.D. Ill.) — Motions and hearings
docs.x: Judge David Wayne Dugan, S.D. Ill.. Motions and hearings: Judge Dugan decides nearly all motions; referral to a magistrate judge happens only rarely or in an emergency, and parties are told through CM/ECF. Local Rule 7.1 deadlines and page limits govern but may be altered in a particular case. The judge may set motions for hearing sua sponte, but not in every case; hearings are in person in East St. Louis unless the court says otherwise. The court welcomes requests for oral argument that would give relatively inexperienced attorneys courtroom experience. If the court orders the parties to arrange a teleconference, counsel must use a professional teleconference provider and split the cost equally unless ordered otherwise.

docs.t: Judge David Wayne Dugan (S.D. Ill.) — Urgent filings and contact (trap)

docs.t: Judge David Wayne Dugan (S.D. Ill.) — Jury selection and deliberations
docs.x: Judge David Wayne Dugan, S.D. Ill.. The court may conduct voir dire without counsel. Cause challenges come first, then a private caucus before peremptories. Leave a phone number with the courtroom deputy during deliberations and be able to reach the courtroom within 10 minutes. No post-verdict juror interviews without the judge’s approval.

docs.t: Judge James Patrick Hanlon (S.D. Ind.) — Filing motions and exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge James Patrick Hanlon, S.D. Ind.. Filing motions and exhibits (trap): File the motion and exhibits before the supporting brief, so the brief can cite their docket numbers. Exhibits may be attached to the motion or filed separately (motion first); a response, reply, or surreply files an appendix or index of exhibits first. Label each exhibit with a number and a descriptive identifier (for example, “Ex. 1 – Smith Dep.”), not just “Exhibit 1.” Cite the docket number, attachment number, and .pdf page from the header (for example, “Dkt. 42-8 at 5”); for depositions, add page and line (“Dkt. 38-2 at 3 (Johnson Dep. at 10:4-13)”).

docs.t: Judge James Patrick Hanlon (S.D. Ind.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge James Patrick Hanlon, S.D. Ind.. Summary judgment (trap): Before moving, contact the other parties to learn whether they also plan to move. If so, four briefs replace the usual schedule: Party A’s motion (30 pages), Party B’s cross-motion and response (45), Party A’s reply and response (30), and Party B’s reply (15). A different process requires a motion stating all counsel’s positions. Motions to exceed page limits and collateral motions such as motions to strike are disfavored; raise evidentiary disputes in the briefs (L.R. 56-1(i)). Cite evidence for every fact in both the fact and argument sections (L.R. 56-1(e)); unsupported facts may be disregarded. Deposition cites need page and line, and the exhibit must include the cited pages plus at least the 3 pages before and after, or the court may decline to consider it.

docs.t: Judge James Patrick Hanlon (S.D. Ind.) — Other motions
docs.x: Judge James Patrick Hanlon, S.D. Ind.. Other motions: If a complaint is amended after a Rule 12 motion, the standard practice is to deny the motion without prejudice as moot. TRO and preliminary injunction motions must also address when the irreparable harm will occur, whether discovery is needed (and what), whether an evidentiary or argument hearing is sought, and a proposed timeline for discovery, hearings, and rulings. Rule 72(a) objections to a magistrate judge’s nondispositive ruling follow the briefing schedule in L.R. 7-1(c)(3). Oral argument on civil motions is granted only in exceptional cases.

docs.x: Judge James Patrick Hanlon, S.D. Ind.. Final pretrial conference: Meet and confer beforehand and be prepared to address pending motions, objections, voir dire, and jury instructions. File motions in limine as one document listing each issue by number; the response must answer each issue “no objection” or “objection” with supporting argument. The agenda typically covers voir dire and argument lengths, witnesses, stipulations, exhibits (bring copies), deposition testimony, motions in limine, preliminary and final instructions, verdict forms, forfeiture in criminal cases, and settlement in civil cases.

docs.t: Judge James Patrick Hanlon (S.D. Ind.) — Depositions at trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge James Patrick Hanlon, S.D. Ind.. Depositions at trial (trap): Deposed medical experts who routinely examine and treat patients are presumed “unavailable” under Rule 32(a)(4), so any party may offer their deposition testimony, even for firsthand observations. A written objection to the presumption must be filed at least 30 days before trial. In bench trials, offer deposition portions as an exhibit rather than reading them; in jury trials, reading (other than for impeachment) should be rare and is done with a reader in the witness box, using a marked transcript offered as an exhibit that does not go to the jury. Video depositions: mark and offer both the video and the marked transcript. For impeachment, identify the page and line orally for the record. Summaries of depositions are allowed only by stipulation.

docs.t: Judge James Patrick Hanlon (S.D. Ind.) — Exhibits
docs.x: Judge James Patrick Hanlon, S.D. Ind.. Each page of each exhibit should bear an identifying number. Provide an electronic file of PDF exhibits by exhibit number one week before trial, and three binders of documentary exhibits at the final pretrial conference. docs.t: Judge Matthew Paul Brookman (S.D. Ind.) — Trial day and courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Matthew Paul Brookman, S.D. Ind.. Trial day and courtroom conduct: The jury typically comes in at 9:00 a.m.; counsel must be in the courtroom by 8:00 a.m. on the first day and at least by 8:30 a.m. after that, and the jury usually leaves around 5:00 p.m. Do not run out of witnesses. Examine from the lectern; stand to object, stating only the ground. Only the lawyer handling a witness’s direct (or cross) may object during the other side’s examination. A plaintiff suggesting a damages number must state it in the opening segment of closing. Phones may be used in session only for text messages coordinating trial logistics. Arrange daily transcripts with the court reporter at least two weeks before trial.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — General expectations
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. General expectations: Counsel must know the Local Rules and the Seventh Circuit Committee on Civility’s Final Report (attached to the procedures, with its Standards for Professional Conduct). Stand when speaking for the record or addressing the court, and use the lectern except for brief objections. No colloquy or argument between attorneys; address all remarks to the court. Avoid first names, and never address a juror individually or by name. Do not ask the reporter to mark testimony or label exhibits; counsel label exhibits, and requests for read-backs go to the court. Contact: Barker_CRD@insd.uscourts.gov or the courtroom deputy at (317) 229-3602.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Phones and devices (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Phones and devices (trap): Cell phones and recording devices of every kind must be turned off, not just silenced, during proceedings, and may not be used in any way while court is in session.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Trial hours and witnesses
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Trial hours and witnesses: Trial usually runs from 9:30 a.m. to about noon and from after lunch to 5:15 p.m., with a midmorning and one midafternoon recess. Have the next witness in the courtroom and ready after any recess. Do not run out of witnesses: a substantial delay may be deemed resting. The court will try to let doctors and other professional witnesses testify out of sequence; discuss it with opposing counsel and, if there is an objection, confer with the court in advance. Give the court and reporter a witness list, with correct spellings, when trial begins.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Jury selection: The venire list, seating chart, and questionnaires are given to counsel the morning of trial. The court conducts voir dire of all potential jurors in a single session; submit any questions the court would not routinely ask in writing before trial. At a sidebar after the court’s questioning, counsel may request follow-up questions and make for-cause challenges. Strikes are made at a sidebar. Criminal: the government strikes 1, the defense 2, alternating, with the government last with 1. Civil: sides alternate single strikes, starting with the plaintiff. In civil cases with more than six jurors, all remaining jurors deliberate.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Exhibits (trap): Mark exhibits before trial and give the court and reporter a list. Plaintiff’s exhibits are numbered; defendant’s are lettered (A–Z, AA, AB, and so on), with contents of a container marked as sub-exhibits (AB-1, AB-2). Large document sets are displayed electronically, so juror notebooks are not needed; make electronically stored exhibits easy to retrieve. Bring your own computer and learn the court’s evidence display system in advance. Confer before trial to stipulate to authenticity and admissibility; stipulated exhibits may be moved in at the outset. Offer other exhibits when they become admissible, and substitute photographs for drugs, counterfeit currency, firearms, and other dangerous items.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Depositions at trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Depositions at trial (trap): Depositions to be used as evidence must be distilled and summarized in writing before trial and exchanged with opposing counsel, who may counter-designate in the same form. The summaries (which may quote significant testimony), not the transcript, may be read to the jury. Any deposition used at trial, as evidence or for impeachment, must be available in the courtroom. Confer to edit written and video depositions.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Jury instructions: File and serve proposed instructions three working days before trial unless the court sets a different schedule. Focus on case-specific instructions, since the court knows the standard ones, and cite authority for each. When possible, also email them in Word or a similar format to the courtroom deputy. The instructions conference is held at the close of the evidence.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Examination and objections
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Examination and objections: Examine from the lectern and stand to object, stating only the ground; argument on an objection only with the court’s permission. Only the lawyer handling the direct (or cross) of a witness may object during the other side’s examination. Ask permission to approach a witness only to consult privately; no permission is needed to work with an exhibit, but face the jury and return to the lectern promptly.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Openings, closings, and advance notice
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Openings, closings, and advance notice: Openings are limited to what the evidence will show. The court will honor reasonable, balanced time requests and expects counsel to confer on any differences. If a legal or evidentiary question is complex, will need extensive argument, or requires a proffer outside the jury’s presence, and conferring has not resolved it, give the court advance notice.

docs.t: Judge Sarah Evans Barker (S.D. Ind.) — Courthouse logistics
docs.x: Judge Sarah Evans Barker, S.D. Ind.. Courthouse logistics: Witnesses should wait in Room 221, down the east hallway from Courtroom 216. Clients and witnesses should avoid the third floor during jury trials, where jurors enter the jury room. Chambers phones and copier are not available to counsel; a copier is available for a per-page fee in the court’s library. After trial begins, give the courtroom deputy copies of documents docketed electronically.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Courtesy copies and hyperlinks
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Courtesy copies and hyperlinks: Courtesy copies to chambers are not necessary. Judge Pratt prefers, but does not require, hyperlinks to cited law and prior CM/ECF filings.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Summary judgment (trap): A party planning to move must ask the other parties whether they also plan to move. If more than one will, the judge prefers four briefs instead of mirror-image briefing: (1) Party A’s motion and brief; (2) Party B’s cross-motion, brief, and response, filed with the Motion for Summary Judgment event, not the Response event; (3) Party A’s reply and response, filed with the Response in Opposition event linked to the cross-motion; and (4) Party B’s reply, filed with the Reply event linked to the cross-motion. Collateral motions such as motions to strike are disfavored; raise evidentiary disputes in the briefs. When relying on a deposition, cite page and line, and file the excerpt plus the three pages immediately before and after each excerpt.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Final pretrial conference
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Final pretrial conference: The agenda covers witness and exhibit lists (bring one copy of proposed exhibits), motions in limine and other pending motions, settlement or plea status, length of voir dire, openings, and closings, preliminary and joint issue instructions (or charging indictment), deposition testimony, stipulations, separation of witnesses, and use of the court’s VEPS system.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Trial day and promptness (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Trial day and promptness (trap): Trials usually run 9:00 a.m. to about 5:00 p.m., with a roughly 10-minute morning break, an hour lunch, and a 15-minute afternoon recess. Be in the courtroom at least 15 minutes before each day’s start and 30 minutes before on the first day. Never be late: the court may resume a jury trial without a party who fails to return on time. Do not run out of witnesses; after a substantial delay the court may deem you rested. The court tries not to hold doctors and other non-party professional witnesses over and will consider taking them out of sequence; discuss with opposing counsel and advise the courtroom deputy of any objection in advance. Only counsel of record with an appearance on file may sit at counsel tables. Electronic devices must be off (not silent or vibrate) in the courtroom; only bottled water is allowed.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Openings, closings, and jury selection
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Openings, closings, and jury selection: Use the lectern. When the court says “two minutes remain,” your time has expired; conclude at once or be cut off. Raise in advance any exhibit, not stipulated as admissible, that you intend to use in opening. A plaintiff’s damages number must be stated in the opening segment of closing, where most of the time must be spent. Be brief. The venire list and questionnaires are available to counsel of record after noon the Friday before trial. Fourteen prospective jurors are seated by draw number. After the court’s voir dire, counsel get up to fifteen minutes per side. Civil: at least three peremptory challenges per side and ordinarily seven jurors, all deliberating, no alternates. Criminal: six for the government and ten for the defense, plus any for alternates. Challenges are simultaneous and in writing.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Witness examination and objections (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Witness examination and objections (trap): Examine from the lectern; no permission is needed to approach a witness to work with an exhibit. Avoid questions that begin “It is my understanding,” recap testimony, seek a “best guess,” include preparatory remarks, ask the witness to agree with counsel, or are negative. Editorial comments on answers may draw a prompt rebuke without private warning. Stand to object, state only the ground, and argue further only with permission. When a party has several lawyers, only the lawyer handling the witness’s direct (or cross) may object during the other side’s examination. The court may allow jurors to submit written questions, reviewed with counsel outside the jury’s hearing; counsel may then follow up.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Exhibits
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Exhibits: Give the courtroom deputy three copies of trial exhibits, in binders tabbed by exhibit number, the Friday before trial, and provide a descriptive exhibit list to the court and court reporter. Number exhibits only (no “Plaintiff’s Exhibit”) under one system agreed at the start of discovery. An exhibit is not admitted until the court admits it on the record in front of the jury; only admitted exhibits may be displayed. Stipulations on admissibility and authenticity are expected; file only stipulations approved by both parties. Arrange oversized exhibits or models with the courtroom deputy at least two weeks before trial, and VEPS use (including by anyone other than counsel of record) at least three weeks before. Exhibits not on 8½” x 11” or 14” x 11” paper are returned to the parties, who must deliver them to the Court of Appeals if needed.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Depositions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Depositions (trap): Deposed treating medical experts and treating health care providers are presumed “unavailable,” so any party may offer their deposition testimony. An objection, showing good cause why deposition-only testimony would be prejudicial, must be filed at least 30 days before trial. Depositions read at trial are read with a person in the witness box; the marked original transcript (and any video) is offered as an exhibit but not sent to the jury. Confer on deposition objections before the final pretrial conference; summaries are allowed only by stipulation.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Jury instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Jury instructions (trap): Counsel must confer and file one joint document of all proposed final instructions, each followed by plaintiff’s and defendant’s objections, including a joint issue instruction, with citations to authority for each. Recent instructions are available from the courtroom deputy. The court holds an on-the-record instructions conference near the close of evidence and gives final instructions before closing; each juror receives a copy of the preliminary and final instructions.

docs.t: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt (S.D. Ind.) — Transcripts and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Tanya Walton Pratt, S.D. Ind.. Transcripts and sentencing: Arrange daily transcripts with the court reporter at least two weeks before trial, and give the reporter a word list the Friday before trial. Criminal: file sentencing memoranda no later than one week before the sentencing hearing, and file letters supporting a defendant in CM/ECF.

docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. The pretrial conference is held in chambers (Suite 814). All counsel who will participate in trial must attend, with full authority to speak for the party and enter stipulations, unless excused (L.U. Civ. R. 16(j)(6)(A)). Pretrial orders follow Local Rule 16(j) and the official form, with two exceptions: the magistrate judge’s signature is waived, and the completed original pretrial order is submitted to Judge Ozerden at the pretrial conference.

docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Settlement memoranda (trap): In jury cases where settlement may be discussed, confer with clients beforehand and have clients, corporate representatives, or adjusters present or available by telephone at the pretrial conference. Send the court a confidential settlement memorandum (3 pages maximum) with a brief explanation of the case and a candid appraisal of positions, including possible settlement figures, by email or mail, to be received at least 3 business days before the pretrial conference. It is not exchanged, not filed, and is destroyed after settlement talks end. Do not submit settlement memoranda in non-jury cases.

docs.t: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden (S.D. Miss.) — Jury instructions and findings
docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Non-jury cases: proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law are due by email in Word 14 calendar days before trial, with copies exchanged between counsel.

docs.t: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden (S.D. Miss.) — Deposition designations (trap)
docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Deposition designations (trap): Depositions offered at trial (other than for rebuttal or impeachment) must be abridged and designated by page and line in the pretrial order under Local Rule 16(j)(5)(A)–(C), with counter-designations and objections identified there. Objections not noted in the pretrial order are waived. The offering party must give the court one color-coded hard copy of each transcript, showing each party’s designations and objections, at least 14 calendar days before the trial setting. For video depositions, the court reviews written transcripts of the objected-to portions; edit videos before trial per Local Rule 16(j)(5)(D).

docs.t: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden (S.D. Miss.) — Motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Motions in limine: Per Local Rule 7(b)(2)(E), motions in limine are due 21 calendar days before the pretrial conference and responses 14 calendar days before. Untimely motions are summarily denied absent good cause.

docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Civil exhibits and witness lists (trap): Email the witness list and exhibit list in Word to the courtroom deputy at ozerden_chambers@mssd.uscourts.gov at least 2 business days before trial, with a copy to opposing counsel. The exhibit list must follow the posted sample format, leaving the sponsor, identification, and evidence columns blank. At the pretrial conference, schedule an exhibit conference with the courtroom deputy, to be held at least 2 business days before trial, to review exhibits and lists jointly before copies are made. Once approved, give the deputy the originals and two copies. In prisoner-complaint trials, bring the exhibit list and exhibits to the pretrial conference and leave them with the deputy. Copies for the court preferably go in a notebook; otherwise staple multi-page exhibits. Number every page in the bottom right corner

Multiple parties with separate exhibits add distinguishing letters (civil, e.g., PM-1) or numbers (criminal, e.g., D(1)-1). List each part of a composite exhibit (P-1a, P-1b) on its own line. docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Defendants and all trial counsel with full authority must attend unless excused in advance for good cause; a defendant with a plea date already arranged may be excused. Notice of a change of plea must be given in writing by the date in the notice; pleas after the stated date are open unless the court grants an extension for good cause, which must be requested before the stated deadline. Proposed jury instructions are due 6 days before trial, emailed in accessible Word format with a copy to opposing counsel, each numbered, separate, bearing the case style and number, with supporting authorities at the bottom. Exhibit and witness lists are also due 6 days before trial; the notice sa

docs.t: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden (S.D. Miss.) — Privacy and record on appeal
docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Privacy and record on appeal: Avoid eliciting Social Security and financial account numbers, minors’ names, birth dates, and (in criminal cases) home addresses at trial; counsel may ask to strike or redact, or the court may do so on its own. Admitted exhibits are scanned and docketed publicly when a notice of appeal is filed, so parties must redact exhibits under the E-Government Act when presenting them.

docs.t: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden (S.D. Miss.) — Sanctions, contact, and courtroom technology
docs.x: Judge Halil Suleyman Ozerden, S.D. Miss.. Sanctions, contact, and courtroom technology: If a party or attorney fails to appear or follow the pretrial order, the court may hold an ex parte hearing and enter dismissal, default, other judgment, or sanctions. Give adequate advance notice before using the courtroom video displays or other presentation technology, and strictly observe the court’s electronic-devices rule. Courtroom deputy questions: (228) 679-1070.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Briefs and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Briefs and page limits (trap): Opening and response briefs are capped at 25 pages and replies at 10 (civil and criminal). Leave to exceed requires good cause and must be sought far enough ahead for the court to rule; an overlong brief filed without leave is summarily stricken. Signature blocks, certificates of service, and tables don’t count. The motion and supporting memorandum must be filed together as one document. 12-point font, one-inch margins, double spacing. Citations to authority, the record, and the docket must be in the text, not in footnotes; footnotes are disfavored and, if used, must be 11-point single-spaced. Skip standard-of-review language in routine motions unless the standard is contested. No ad hominem attacks in briefs; the court will not tolerate rudeness or bullying, in or out of court.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Remote appearances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Remote appearances (trap): All proceedings are in person unless the hearing notice says otherwise. A written motion to appear by Zoom is due at least 4 days before the appearance, after conferring with opposing counsel, and must state whether they consent and the specific grounds. Remote participants must use a quiet room with a stable internet connection; headsets are encouraged.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Continuances and extensions
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Continuances and extensions: Move in writing with grounds, after conferring; state whether the other side consents and give jointly proposed new dates (or explain why the parties couldn’t agree). If the motion is filed within 3 business days of the proceeding or deadline, moving counsel must also call chambers at (614) 719-3250. Criminal: a continuance in a case not yet set for trial may be requested orally at a telephone status conference, stating the reason, whether the time is excludable under the Speedy Trial Act, and whether the defendant knows of and objects to it. The government is responsible for Speedy Trial Act compliance and may be ordered to submit a calculation.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Depositions, sealing, and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Depositions, sealing, and proposed orders: Civil: a party citing a deposition must file the entire deposition on ECF; sealing a deposition requires leave first. Sealing requires a motion for leave on the docket showing the request meets Shane Group’s strict standards. In criminal cases, also email the motion, a proposed order, and the document for in-camera review to Cole_Chambers@ohsd.uscourts.gov. Proposed orders on unopposed motions are appreciated; file them on ECF and email them to Cole_Chambers@ohsd.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Specific motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Specific motions (trap): Supplemental authority is disfavored; file it only if it is both new and binding (Sixth Circuit or Supreme Court). Daubert motions (and, in criminal cases, motions to suppress) are filed separately at least 20 days before the final pretrial conference unless a trial scheduling order says otherwise. Responses are due 10 days after filing; no replies unless ordered; the page limits apply. The court may hold a hearing. After filing a TRO motion, counsel must contact chambers to request an informal conference (S.D. Ohio Civ. R. 65.1(a)).

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Newer attorneys
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Newer attorneys: Any party may file a notice that, if oral argument is granted, a newer attorney (six or fewer years of practice) will argue some or all of the motion; the court will set argument if at all practicable. Opposing counsel need not match, and the court draws no inference either way.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Accommodations
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Accommodations: Send accommodation requests to Cole_Chambers@ohsd.uscourts.gov, not through ECF.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Criminal: Brady
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Criminal: Brady: The government has a continuing duty to timely produce favorable, material evidence. Information it considers favorable but not material must be submitted to the court for in-camera review.

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Trial schedule and jury
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Trial schedule and jury: Trial runs Monday through Friday: 9:30 a.m. to about 5 p.m., with breaks around 11 a.m. and 3:30 p.m., lunch around 12:15 to 1:15 p.m. Civil counsel must be in the courtroom a half hour before the start. Enter appearances with the court reporter and deputy on arrival. Civil: 8 jurors, unanimous verdict, no verdict from fewer than 6 unless stipulated. Each party gets 3 peremptories, exercised alternately (plaintiff first) only against jurors in the box; a pass counts as used. Criminal: peremptories per Rule 24, government first, with the defendant offering two per turn in a felony case; a pass counts as used. Alternates are then picked the same way. The whole panel is examined in one continuous voir dire. The court questions first; counsel may supplement without repeating, must address the whole panel, refer to jurors by number, a

docs.t: Judge Douglas R. Cole (S.D. Ohio) — Courtroom conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge Douglas R. Cole, S.D. Ohio. Courtroom conduct (trap): Examine witnesses, give openings and closings, and address the court from the lectern, standing. Ask permission to approach a witness (and, in civil cases, the bench) and to confer with co-counsel; one lawyer per witness. Re-cross is generally not allowed. Object by stating only the objection and legal grounds; no speeches, and no argument unless the court asks. No colloquy between counsel, no first names, and don’t ask the reporter to mark testimony. Civil: show demonstratives to opposing counsel one week before trial and submit objections before trial starts; closing-only demonstratives at the earliest time, no later than a half hour before argument. Bring your own easel and flip charts. Noncompliance can draw sanctions, including monetary sanctions, dismissal of claims or defenses, or exclusion of evidence.

docs.t: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr. (S.D. Ohio) — Trial setting and continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr., S.D. Ohio. Trial setting and continuances (trap): The court uses a trailing docket, setting three to five civil cases to start on the same day and trying them in the order filed. If an earlier case goes to trial, the next case must stay ready on standby for two weeks unless the court orders otherwise. Criminal matters set at the same time get preference. The civil trial date will not be continued except on a written motion supported by an affidavit showing exceptional circumstances, made immediately on learning of them. A date that falls on a weekend or legal holiday moves to the next business day.

docs.x: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr., S.D. Ohio. Settlement conference with the judge (trap): Jury cases get a settlement conference before Judge Sargus personally (none in non-jury cases). The trial attorney must attend, and parties or principals with settlement authority must be present. Lack of discovery, or pending dispositive motions, does not excuse active participation. Each plaintiff must serve a fully documented written demand at least 14 days before the conference; each opposing party must respond in writing, fully documented, at least 10 days before. On the date set, each party emails a confidential assessment letter of no more than 3 pages (theory of the case, settlement position in monetary terms if applicable, and all conditions for settlement) only to Sargus_Chambers@ohsd.uscourts.gov. Counsel must also discuss with clients whether a summary jury trial or other ADR fits (S.D. Ohio C

docs.t: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr. (S.D. Ohio) — Citation of authority (trap)
docs.x: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr., S.D. Ohio. Citation of authority (trap): On federal law the court strongly prefers citations only to the U.S. Constitution, federal statutes, rules, treaties, or regulations, the Supreme Court, and the Sixth Circuit. Non-binding authority should be cited only if nothing binding is on point; otherwise put it in an appendix of supplemental authorities with a parenthetical for each, and prefer other circuits’ decisions. On Ohio law, cite the Ohio Constitution, the Revised Code, the Ohio Supreme Court, and Sixth Circuit decisions construing Ohio law, then published Ohio appellate decisions if nothing binding exists. docs.x: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr., S.D. Ohio. The court may hold a hearing first. A party’s motions in limine and supporting memoranda may not exceed 10 pages in total, and oppositions likewise 10 pages. No replies are accepted. No trial briefs unless ordered.

docs.t: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr. (S.D. Ohio) — Pretrial submissions
docs.x: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr., S.D. Ohio. Pretrial submissions: By the dates in the scheduling order, file and serve witness lists (name, address, occupation, a 2–3 sentence summary, its purpose, and the main issue), deposition designations (not portions used only to impeach), and exhibit lists. Unlisted witnesses and undesignated deposition portions are excluded absent good cause. Agreed exhibits are marked as Joint Exhibits. One copy of exhibits in a three-ring, tabbed notebook goes to the courtroom deputy (Christin Werner) at least 2 days before trial. docs.t: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr. (S.D. Ohio) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Edmund A. Sargus Jr., S.D. Ohio. Jury instructions: The court prepares the preliminary and general instructions (posted on its page); parties should focus on case-specific instructions. Serve proposed instructions and verdict forms, confer, and submit one joint set with an agreed common index. Where the parties disagree, plaintiff’s version appears first, immediately followed by defendant’s, on one page for comparison, with pinpoint citations to binding authority in footnotes. Serve discovery so responses are due before the cutoff. A pending motion does not suspend discovery deadlines. docs.t: Judge Michael R. Barrett (S.D. Ohio) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Michael R. Barrett, S.D. Ohio. The preliminary pretrial conference, usually by phone, is within 60 days after all counsel are identified. The judge generally allows 6 months of discovery and requires plaintiff’s expert reports 30 to 45 days before defendant’s. No more than 5 experts per disclosure without permission. All deadlines are firm, and the court will impose sanctions, including monetary sanctions. Attorney fee motions (absent a stipulation) need an itemized affidavit and are due 45 days after judgment (S.D. Ohio Civ. R. 54.2).

docs.x: Judge Michael R. Barrett, S.D. Ohio. Settlement: The court may set a settlement conference at any time, and counsel may request one. Each party submits a confidential ex parte letter of no more than 5 pages (positions, case synopsis, negotiation status) 7 days before the conference, delivered or emailed to chambers and not filed.

Cross-motions submitting the whole case vacate the pretrial and trial dates.

docs.t: Judge Sarah D. Morrison (S.D. Ohio) — Opportunities for newer attorneys
docs.x: Judge Sarah D. Morrison, S.D. Ohio. docs.t: Judge Sarah D. Morrison (S.D. Ohio) — Joint final pretrial statement (civil)
docs.x: Judge Sarah D. Morrison, S.D. Ohio. Joint final pretrial statement (civil): Use the judge’s Joint Final Pre-Trial Statement template. Estimate trial length including voir dire, and give each witness’s name, address, occupation (for professional witnesses), and a brief synopsis. Rebuttal witnesses of doubtful character must be disclosed 5 days before trial or they will not be allowed to testify. Unlisted witnesses and exhibits are excluded except for impeachment or good cause. Attach expert CVs as Exhibit A and separate exhibit lists (Exhibits B–E: joint, plaintiff, defendant, third-party), with each exhibit on only one list and any objection’s nature and authority noted. State whether a jury view is requested.

docs.t: Judge Sarah D. Morrison (S.D. Ohio) — Trial practice
docs.x: Judge Sarah D. Morrison, S.D. Ohio. Trial practice: Trials run Monday to Friday: 9 a.m. to noon and 1 to 5 p.m., with short morning and afternoon recesses. Enter your appearance with the court reporter and courtroom deputy before each proceeding starts. Plaintiff or the government takes the table next to the jury box. Address the court and jury from the lectern and stand to address the court. Ask permission to approach a witness or the bench and to confer with co-counsel; only one attorney per side may examine a given witness, and re-cross is generally not allowed. Object by standing and stating the legal grounds only; argument only at the court’s request. Show demonstratives to opposing counsel one week before trial, with objections submitted before trial starts; closing-only aids at least half an hour before closings. Bring your own easels and flip charts.

docs.t: Judge Sarah D. Morrison (S.D. Ohio) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Sarah D. Morrison, S.D. Ohio. Jury selection: Civil juries have 8 members; the verdict must be unanimous and from no fewer than 6 jurors unless the parties stipulate otherwise. The whole panel is examined and challenged in one continuous process, and jurors are referred to by number. Do not copy or circulate the juror questionnaires. Civil: 3 peremptory challenges per party, alternating with plaintiff first, directed only at jurors in the box; a pass counts as used. Criminal: peremptories follow Rule 24, the government goes first, and in a felony case the defendant exercises two per turn; a pass counts as used.

docs.x: Judge Andrew Hanen, S.D. Tex.. Conference certificates and Rule 12 motions (trap): Every pretrial motion needs a certificate of conference. docs.x: Judge Andrew Hanen, S.D. Tex.. docs.t: Judge Andrew Hanen (S.D. Tex.) — Emergencies and continuances
docs.x: Judge Andrew Hanen, S.D. Tex.. Emergencies and continuances: TROs and other emergency applications go through the clerk’s office and are presented via the Case Manager after counsel affirms the opposing party was contacted and both sides can attend a conference. Ex parte TROs are discouraged and require full Rule 65(b) compliance. Also send the Case Manager a file-stamped hard copy of any emergency motion. The Rule 26(f) meeting must be held in person, by phone, or by video; email meetings are not allowed.

Parties may agree to extend discovery and expert deadlines without approval if the dispositive-motion deadline and docket call are unaffected; changing those requires a motion, and agreed continuance motions don’t bind the court. Vacation requests made well in advance are respected. In-person attendance is preferred. docs.t: Judge Jeff Brown (S.D. Tex.) — Amended pleadings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jeff Brown, S.D. Tex.. Amended pleadings (trap): Amended pleadings must reproduce the entire pleading, with no incorporation by reference without leave. A motion or stipulation to amend must attach a redline showing every change (strikethrough for deletions, underlining for additions); once leave is granted, file and serve the clean version within 14 days of the order. Under the docket-control order form, pleadings may be amended without leave until the amendment deadline; after that, a motion showing good cause under Rule 16(b)(4) is required. In removed cases, adding new parties always requires a motion for leave.

docs.t: Judge Jeff Brown (S.D. Tex.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jeff Brown, S.D. Tex.. Pretrial (trap): No joint pretrial order. At least 24 hours before docket call (9:30 a.m.), each party separately files its exhibit list, witness list, proposed voir dire, proposed jury instructions, motions in limine, and deposition designations and objections, and delivers 2 tabbed binders of those filings and 2 tabbed binders of its exhibits. Exchange proposed motions in limine, exhibit lists, and deposition designations at least 1 week before docket call, and confer to narrow the issues. Docket call is the final pretrial conference; the case is set for trial on a date certain within the next 60 days. Pretrial authenticity and admissibility objections follow Local Rules 44 and 46, and Rule 11 applies to authenticity objections. The court tries to rule on objections and admit as many exhibits as possible before trial.

docs.t: Judge Jeff Brown (S.D. Tex.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jeff Brown, S.D. Tex.. Trial: The court conducts a preliminary voir dire, and each side may briefly examine the panel if proposed questions were properly submitted. The parties may agree to use a deposition even if the witness is available. Don’t “tender” an expert to the court for recognition of expertise; all such tenders are refused. Bench trials follow the same pretrial filings; the parties must file proposed findings and conclusions, and the court may allow post-trial briefs instead of closings or require findings before trial.

docs.t: Judge Jeff Brown (S.D. Tex.) — Settlement and special matters
docs.x: Judge Jeff Brown, S.D. Tex.. Settlement and special matters: Call the case manager when settlement is contemplated so pending motions can be held, and report settlement immediately. Every settlement announcement draws a conditional dismissal, without prejudice to reinstatement within 60 days. A minor plaintiff’s settlement with a parent conflict requires a joint motion to appoint a guardian ad litem. Social security appeals must be opened using only the claimant’s initials in the last-name field. Initial ex parte admiralty motions go to Judge Edison, with Word proposed orders emailed to Judge Edison’s case manager. In criminal cases, motions to suppress must be filed before the pretrial conference unless ordered otherwise.

docs.t: Judge Lee H. Rosenthal (S.D. Tex.) — Discovery objections (trap)

A response “subject to” objections must say whether it is complete and, if anything is withheld because of the objections, give enough information about what was withheld to allow further inquiry. A partial production must state whether and when more will be produced. Requests must meet Rule 26(b)(1) relevance and proportionality; parties may not over-ask, or object and withhold needed material, for strategic or tactical reasons.

docs.t: Judge Lee H. Rosenthal (S.D. Tex.) — Motions and briefs
docs.x: Judge Lee H. Rosenthal, S.D. Tex.. Motions and briefs: Dispositive and other motions generally follow the Local Rules’ written motion practice and are considered after the submission date. Oral argument must be requested in writing with an explanation of why it would help. Briefs are limited to 25 pages without leave. Every brief must include a statement of the nature and stage of the proceeding, the issues and standard of review for each with authority, informative headings, and a short conclusion stating the precise relief; briefs with more than 10 pages of argument also need tables of contents and authorities and a summary of argument. Parties may agree to extend a motion submission date without leave unless that breaches a court-ordered deadline; notify the case manager in writing immediately

docs.x: Judge Lee H. Rosenthal, S.D. Tex.. Unless counsel has actually begun trial elsewhere, other trial settings won’t delay a case set for trial. docs.t: Judge Lee H. Rosenthal (S.D. Tex.) — Trial days and courtroom
docs.x: Judge Lee H. Rosenthal, S.D. Tex.. Trial days and courtroom: Court normally runs 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. with about a 45-minute lunch; counsel should arrive earlier and stay later than the jury. The court conducts preliminary voir dire, then each side may examine the panel. Counsel may question from counsel table or a lectern. The court generally won’t recess for a missing witness unless the witness was subpoenaed and failed to appear. Counsel table seating is first-come, first-served on the first day; use only the front doors. No contact with jurors after discharge except as the court permits.

The rule applies to pro se litigants too.

docs.t: Judge Nicholas Ganjei (S.D. Tex.) — Trial

docs.x: Judge S. Maurice Hicks Jr., W.D. La.. docs.t: Judge S. Maurice Hicks Jr. (W.D. La.) — Pretrial order contents
docs.x: Judge S. Maurice Hicks Jr., W.D. La.. Pretrial order contents: Stipulated facts are listed by number. Each contested fact and issue of law must be stated as a concise narrative of each party’s contention, never solely as a question. In a direct action against an insurer, identify the insured. Edit irrelevant material out of depositions before trial; complete, unedited transcripts will not be admitted. State whether the case is jury or non-jury (and which issues go to the jury), the expected length, and whether liability should be tried separately from quantum. The order must be prepared at a face-to-face or telephone conference including trial counsel for all parties, and once entered it controls trial and can be changed only by consent of the parties and the court or to prevent manifest injustice.

docs.t: Judge S. Maurice Hicks Jr. (W.D. La.) — Rule 26(f) case management report
docs.x: Judge S. Maurice Hicks Jr., W.D. La.. A proposed amendment deadline more than 30 days after the scheduling conference, or a discovery completion deadline more than 5 months after it, needs a detailed explanation. Absent stipulation or leave, the court enforces the FRCP discovery limits: 10 depositions per side, one day of 7 hours per deposition, and 25 interrogatories per party. Each party must describe anticipated discovery disputes and the relief it will seek.

docs.x: Judge Brian Curtis Wimes, W.D. Mo.. Scheduling order deadlines (trap): The sample orders set trial no more than 20 months after service of the complaint, close all discovery 180 days after service of the complaint, and set the final pretrial teleconference 30 days before trial, with dispositive motions due at least 120 days before that conference. Discovery must be completed, not just served, by the closure date. In jury cases, Daubert motions are due on the dispositive-motion deadline; missing it waives any Daubert argument (motions in limine on expert testimony are not covered). Defendants designate experts 30 days after plaintiffs. In class actions, the court sets a telephone conference 90 days after the class-certification reply deadline to set trial and related dates; class-related expert designations and class discovery follow the same pattern.

Do not call chambers except in an urgent situation (e.g., an ill attorney will miss a hearing); never call for legal advice or case updates. docs.t: Judge David Gregory Kays (W.D. Mo.) — Briefing rules (trap)
docs.x: Judge David Gregory Kays, W.D. Mo.. Briefing rules (trap): For every motion and brief, primarily cite binding, on-point authority (Eighth Circuit, Supreme Court, or state supreme court on state-law issues). If none exists, affirm in a footnote that you searched thoroughly and found none. Use pinpoint citations to the exact supporting page; Bluebook preferred unless the Local Rules say otherwise. Do not put all citations in footnotes. Never incorporate by reference arguments or facts from prior briefs (it is treated as evading page limits). Violations can mean denial of the motion, a stricken brief, waiver, or sanctions. These rules don’t apply to routine motions (non-scheduling-order extensions, pro hac vice, protective orders).

docs.t: Judge David Gregory Kays (W.D. Mo.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge David Gregory Kays, W.D. Mo.. Discovery disputes (trap): No discovery motion without full compliance with Local Rule 37.1; noncompliant motions are summarily denied. Email the courtroom deputy (Tracy_Strodtman@mow.uscourts.gov), copying the other side, with a short explanation and a certification of Rule 37.1 compliance to request a telephone conference. Each party files a position memorandum of no more than 500 words at least 72 hours before the call, with pinpoint Eighth Circuit citations and the disputed request attached; optional replies of no more than 300 words are due 48 hours before. The court may cancel the call and rule on the papers. Discovery motions are due 4 weeks before the discovery deadline (2 weeks in the 2015 non-jury template); problems not raised in time for a ruling before the close of discovery are waived except in extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Judge David Gregory Kays (W.D. Mo.) — Discovery conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge David Gregory Kays, W.D. Mo.. Discovery conduct (trap): Boilerplate objections in written discovery are deemed waived; each objection must say specifically how the request is deficient and how the party would be harmed by answering. No speaking or coaching objections at depositions (e.g., “answer—if you know”); say only “objection; form” or “objection; vague” unless the examiner asks for an explanation. At the start, deposing counsel must instruct the witness to ask deposing counsel, not the witness’s own counsel, for any clarification, and the witness must comply. Objections are preserved and must not be made during the deposition, except those waived if not made under Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(3)(B) and those needed to assert a privilege, enforce a court-ordered limitation on evidence, or present a Rule 30(d) motion. Objections must be succinct, state only the basis, and not suggest an answer. docs.t: Judge Leslie G. Foschio (W.D.N.Y.) — Deposition guidelines: documents and questioning
docs.x: Judge Leslie G. Foschio, W.D.N.Y.. Deposition guidelines: documents and questioning: Deposing counsel must give the witness’s counsel a copy of every document shown to the witness, either before the deposition or as each document is shown. The witness and counsel have no right to discuss documents privately before the witness answers questions about them. One question at a time; let the witness answer fully without interruption; no characterization of or comment on answers. If an answer seems unresponsive, say so and have the stenographer repeat the question; if a question is unclear, the examiner may rephrase or withdraw it. No argument between counsel over objections or the nature of questions; note the objection on the record and seek relief after the examination. Avoid unnecessary on-the-record recitation or lengthy quotation of documents.
